The core operator 'Dual Team Scoring Prediction' operates on a binary classification task where input features X represent match-specific attributes such as team form, historical head-to-head records, and player availability. The target variable y encodes whether both teams scored goals in a given match. This setup enables a probabilistic framework where P(y=1|X) represents the likelihood of dual scoring. The underlying assumption is that past match data contains sufficient statistical signals to infer future outcomes. The ML framework integrates multiple classifiers—KNN, SVM, DT, LR—to evaluate which algorithm best captures the decision boundary separating dual-scoring from non-dual-scoring instances. Each classifier's performance is evaluated using metrics like confusion matrix, micro-average, macro-average, and F1 score. These metrics quantify how effectively the model distinguishes between classes, thereby enabling robust predictions. The temporal aspect of the Portuguese league data introduces a dynamic element where historical trends must be accounted for in model training and validation. As such, the system must adapt to evolving patterns while maintaining generalizability. Failure modes include overfitting due to insufficient data or misalignment between training and test distributions, and underfitting when the model lacks complexity to capture relevant features. The derived kernel approach in SVM and KNN provides geometric insights into class separability, while decision trees offer interpretable rule structures. Ultimately, this constitutes a dual-state inference engine for football match outcomes, embedded within a broader machine learning architecture.
